criteria.descriptor: Correctly and precisely uses drift taxonomy (covariate P(X) vs concept P(Y|X) vs label/prior P(Y)); accurately describes what PSI measures and its 0.1/0.2 heuristic and limitations; and names valid label-free methods (KS/JS/MMD, confidence-based performance estimation, calibration) without technical errors such as claiming PSI detects concept drift or that accuracy can be computed live.

Covers all three requested parts — (a) what PSI does/doesn't imply, (b) determining real degradation under the label delay, (c) false-alarm control and root-causing — and includes the label-free estimation path, the delayed-label backfill/confirmation, and remediation decisioning rather than stopping at drift detection.

Justifies why input drift is not equivalent to degradation, why each chosen signal/test is appropriate given no fresh labels, and why false-alarm controls (persistence, FDR, seasonality, segmentation) and root-cause checks are needed before retraining; trade-offs are argued, not merely asserted.

Reads as a clear, well-organized design-review response with correct terminology used naturally; a reviewer can act on it. Structure around the three parts and concrete named tools/methods aids clarity.

expected_answer_points: Distinguishes covariate/data drift (P(X)) from concept drift (P(Y|X)) and label/prior drift (P(Y)), and states PSI on inputs detects only P(X) — which is neither sufficient nor necessary for quality degradation (robust models absorb input drift; concept drift degrades quality with no input drift).

Explains PSI mechanics correctly (binned reference-vs-current comparison, ~0.1 moderate / ~0.2 large heuristic thresholds) and its limitations: univariate/ignores feature correlations, binning- and threshold-sensitive, and inflated false-alarm rate when many features are monitored.

Recognizes the 30-day label delay means live accuracy/F1 cannot be measured, so proposes label-free/proxy signals: output-score distribution and predicted class-prior shift, confidence/calibration drift, and embedding-level drift via KS test, Jensen-Shannon divergence, or MMD.

Proposes a label-free performance estimate (e.g. confidence-based performance estimation / NannyML CBPE or DLE) and/or fast partial ground truth via human-labeling a stratified sample of the drifted slice or a canary, to estimate quality before the delayed labels arrive.

Controls false alarms: clean reference window, require sustained/persistent shift over multiple windows (not a single spike), apply multiple-comparison correction (FDR/Bonferroni), account for seasonality, and slice by segment rather than one global alarm.
Closes the loop with the delayed labels: backfill true accuracy on drifted cohorts and confirm statistical and practical significance / business impact before acting.

Applies root-cause discipline: rule out upstream pipeline/schema/feature-encoding changes before concluding genuine population shift, and choose remediation (retrain, rollback, fix, or no-op) accordingly rather than reflexively retraining on an input-drift alarm.
common_pitfalls: Treats the PSI trip as equivalent to model degradation and recommends immediate retraining without any evidence accuracy actually dropped.
Assumes accuracy/F1 can be measured on current traffic, ignoring the 30-day label delay, and proposes computing supervised metrics on data that has no labels yet.
Only monitors inputs and never the model's output-score distribution, predicted-prior, or confidence/calibration — missing pure concept drift that leaves P(X) unchanged.
Confuses concept drift with covariate drift, or claims PSI (an input-distribution metric) can detect concept drift or a P(Y|X) change.

Ignores the multiple-comparisons/false-alarm problem: treats a single PSI spike on one of many features as conclusive, with no persistence requirement, FDR/Bonferroni correction, or seasonality check.
Skips root-causing — never checks for upstream pipeline/schema/feature-encoding changes that masquerade as 'drift' before concluding a genuine population shift.
reference_answer:
The core error to avoid is equating input drift with quality loss. Three distinct shifts matter: covariate/data drift (P(X) changes), label/prior drift (P(Y) changes), and concept drift (P(Y|X) changes — the input→label mapping itself moves). PSI measures only P(X): it bins a reference and current window and sums (curr%-ref%)*ln(curr%/ref%) per bin, with >0.1 a moderate and >0.2 a large shift by convention. So a trip tells me a feature distribution moved — not that accuracy dropped. A robust model can absorb input drift with no quality loss, and pure concept drift can crater accuracy with zero input drift, so PSI is neither sufficient nor necessary evidence of degradation. PSI is also univariate (misses correlation/interaction shifts), binning- and threshold-heuristic, and with many features monitored the odds at least one trips by chance are high.

Because labels lag 30 days I cannot compute live accuracy/F1, so I add label-free signals: the model's output-score distribution and predicted class-prior, confidence and calibration drift (e.g. reliability/ECE over time), and embedding-level drift via the KS test, Jensen-Shannon divergence, or MMD on representations. For an actual quality estimate before labels land I would use confidence-based performance estimation (e.g. NannyML CBPE, or DLE) and buy fast partial ground truth — human-label a stratified sample of the drifted slice, or route a canary. When the delayed labels arrive I backfill true accuracy on the drifted cohorts and confirm the drop is statistically and practically significant.

To control false alarms I fix a clean, representative reference window, require the shift to persist across several consecutive windows rather than firing on one spike, apply multiple-comparison control (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR or Bonferroni) across features, account for known seasonality, and slice by segment instead of a single global alarm. For streaming I would consider ADWIN/DDM/Page-Hinkley. Root-cause discipline comes before action: rule out upstream pipeline/schema/feature-encoding changes (the most common false 'drift') before concluding a genuine population shift, then choose remediation — retrain, rollback, prompt/feature fix, or no-op. Reflexively retraining on an input-PSI alarm alone is the anti-pattern. Tools: Evidently or NannyML for drift/performance-estimation reporting, wired to alerting.
